extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in wartime news, labor and government policy
extracted.subtask_description: A newspaper report summarizing wartime government policies, enforcement procedures, and administrative standards (manpower allocation, transportation enforcement, appeals for paper allotments, and military decoration citations). The page is a multi-item news article aimed at informing the public about rules, procedures and decisions affecting wartime production and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for granting appeals for extra paper tonnage
rubrics_metrics.description: W.P.B. issued revised lists of standards by which appeals for extra paper tonnage from newspaper, book and magazine publishers will be decided. Appeals are granted only to provide relief from undue and excessive hardship which would be created if the order were applied without modification to an exceptional set of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The revised supplement listed specific factors to be taken into consideration in considering appeals for extra tonnage for newspapers: 1. Extraordinary growth of population in the newspaper’s trading area since Jan. 1, 1943, requiring additional paper in order to maintain adequate newspaper service to the community. 2. Discontinuance or merger of newspapers requiring adjustments in the quotas of other newspapers in the trading area in order to maintain adequate newspaper service to the community. 3. Any other unforeseen, unusual, extraordinary or emergency conditions which may constitute undue and excessive hardship. Appeals which do not contain proof establishing this type of hardship will not be granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manpower reallocation and forced lay-offs procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The country has been divided into four groups of labor areas according to labor supply (Group 1 most critically short; Group 4 may have plenty). In labor-shortage areas the Government can force employers to fire or reassign workers whom it believes could be better used elsewhere in war production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational procedure and enforcement: production urgency committees decide the relative importance to war production of plants in each area; manpower priorities committees then decide which plants will get manpower, need less manpower, or should be forced to lay off workers. Sanctions for noncompliance (per Byrnes' guidance) may include shutting off materials, power, fuel, transportation — effectively forcing a business to close until it complies. The War Manpower Commission (WMC) and United States Employment Service offices may refuse to refer or provide workers to noncompliant employers until their staff is reduced to the government-imposed ceiling. Manpower ceilings may be placed on war industries to compel better use of manpower and on less essential industries to reduce their staffs (example given: an employer with 100 men might be told he 'needs only 75' and cannot hire more until his total staff falls to 75). While a worker could technically refuse reassignment under this system (unlike a military draft), refusal may make it difficult for the worker to obtain government permission to remain in the prior job.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back-to-work enforcement and cancellation of occupational deferments
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to strikes disrupting vital transportation, the Government may cancel occupational deferments (selective service deferments) and issue back-to-work orders requiring employees to return to their regular posts by a specified deadline; noncompliance can lead to firing and substitution of military personnel to operate essential services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Philadelphia transit strike: War authorities announced cancellation of occupational deferments of all involved in the strike and ordered that non-returning strikers 'would be fired at once' and that 'soldiers will be used ... to operate vehicles which otherwise would remain idle.' The Army said soldiers would serve as guards on buses, trolleys and trains and operate vehicles where necessary; federal law enforcement (FBI, Department of Justice) was authorized to seek warrants under the Smith-Connally Act against strike leaders. In practice units were mobilized, later demobilized when situation stabilized; authorities described some military deployment as a 'practice drill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Smith-Connally Act violation criteria and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Warrants were issued charging certain individuals with violations of the Smith-Connally Act based on actions that interfered with wartime transportation and production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The warrants specifically charged named persons with 'knowingly, unlawfully coercing, inducing and encouraging certain employes of the Philadelphia Transportation company to interfere by strike and other interruptions with the operation of the company.' The Justice Department and FBI were authorized to invoke the Act. Conviction under the stated charges carries a maximum penalty of a $5,000 fine, one year imprisonment, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria/reasons cited for awarding naval/military decorations
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of decorations awarded to Commodore Campbell D. Edgar and the reasons for each recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decorations awarded and cited reasons (as reported): Medal — for landing an Army command (?) during the invasion of North Africa, November 1942; Gold Star in lieu of a second (citation context incomplete in text); Legion of Merit — for service as commander of transports of a task force, northwest African waters, for operations in the Mediterranean; Army Distinguished Service (oak leaf cluster) — for work as chief of the Allied Military Government section of the American army in Italy, and for serving as commander of transports during the Allied invasion of Italy in September and October, 1943; British Certificate of Appreciation — for cooperation in planning and carrying out landings and operations. (The report lists the medal titles and the operational achievements cited as the grounds for each award.)
